title: Aggrega Workspace Config
description: Per-workspace configuration file consumed by the aggrega CLI. Lives at `.aggrega-config.yaml`. The `workspace` block is the root marker: its presence marks the workspace root, and it holds only `catalog_dirs`. Every other key is a setting and lives at the top level, in these classes — where content is fetched from and cached (registry selection, offline and auto-pull behaviour, artifact and compiled-module cache locations and size caps), how content is trusted (signing, and signature-verification behaviour), how strictly authoring is judged (per-rule lint dials, deprecation strictness, and the authoring-release hint), which Wasm plugins are attached workspace-wide (governance, linter, importer, and per-target provider-rendering bindings), and how the CLI runs (concurrency, serving, and daemon parse-cache eviction caps). The properties below are the complete and authoritative list; this summary names the classes rather than the keys, so adding a key cannot falsify it. Flat top-level shape, no apiVersion/kind envelope, distinct from catalog content. Schema evolution discipline: adding a new top-level key is a SemVer-MINOR bump (additive); removing or relocating a key, or tightening a constraint, is a SemVer-MAJOR break.

workspace.description: Workspace root marker. Its PRESENCE marks the directory as the workspace root; it carries only the root-defining catalog directories. Every setting that is not root-defining lives at the top level rather than here. Write `workspace: {}` to mark a root with no vendored catalog directories.

catalog_dirs.description: Optional catalog directories this workspace reads local entities from, consulted before falling back to the registry. Each entry is a filesystem path, resolved relative to the file that declares it. The list is an ordered first-win search stack: the earliest-listed directory to declare an identity owns it, and the same identity in a later directory is shadowed. The `catalog` directory at the workspace root is read as well, after every listed entry and only when it exists — unless a listed entry already contains it, in which case it is read as part of that entry — so listing a directory adds to what the workspace already read rather than replacing it. Omitting this key and writing it as an empty list are different statements: omitted, the workspace still reads `catalog`; written as `[]`, it reads no local catalog at all, which is how a workspace says it has none. Root-scoped: local catalog directories belong to this workspace root, so they live on the root marker rather than at the top level.

catalog_dirs_append.description: Optional append-only addition to the effective `catalog_dirs` list. At each precedence layer the entries here are concatenated onto the resolved base list, letting workspace and global configs compose catalog directories rather than shadow them. Same-layer interaction: when both `catalog_dirs` and `catalog_dirs_append` are specified at one layer, the resolved value at that layer is the base list followed by the append list.

default_registry.description: Default OCI registry host the build pushes published artifacts to and pulls dependencies from when an entity does not name a registry explicitly. Defaults to `hub.aggrega.ai`.

offline.description: When true, the build does not contact any registry; only cached artifacts and vendored catalog content are consulted. Defaults to false.

auto_pull.description: When false (default), `aggrega build` is read-only: it never writes source pins, and a missing or incomplete per-release lockfile halts the build loudly with a diagnostic to run `aggrega pull --release <release>` first. When true, `aggrega build` runs a pull step in-process before building — resolving the Release's dependencies into the lockfile and cache — so a first-time build against a Release does not require an explicit pull step. The same single-build opt-in is available on the command line as `aggrega build --auto-pull`; `pull` remains the sole writer of source pins. Independent of `offline`: `offline: true` ignores `auto_pull` and always halts on a missing lockfile because the pull step needs network access.

artifact_cache_dir.description: Local artifact/content cache directory (registry pulls, OCI manifests, compiled fixtures). Defaults to `.aggrega/cache`. Should be gitignored by convention. The path is interpreted relative to the workspace root, wherever the command is run from; an absolute value is refused when the configuration loads, because every reader of this setting resolves it against that root and an absolute path would name a location they never reach. The cache may sit inside a catalog directory — the default does, since a catalog directory commonly is the workspace root — but it must not BE one: a catalog scan steps over the cache, so a value naming a catalog directory leaves that directory's entire contents out of the scan. A value naming the workspace root itself (`.`, or any spelling that reduces to it) is refused when the configuration loads, for exactly that reason. A value naming any other catalog directory is not refused: it loads cleanly and the scan then finds nothing in that directory, so keeping the cache out of the directories listed in `workspace.catalog_dirs` is yours to check. Distinct from `parse_cache`, which caps the daemon's in-memory parse cache, and from `compiled_module_cache`, which caps the machine-wide compiled-module store.

skip_signature_verification.description: Global, loud opt-out from signature verification. When true, signature verification is disabled across every registry, including the mandatory hub baseline. Intended for break-glass and development scenarios; it is never silent — every pull logs a prominent warning that verification was globally disabled. Defaults to false.

build.description: Build-time strictness dials and authoring hints. `authoring_release` provides the LSP a `current Release` hint for inline diagnostics; `halt_on_deprecated_severity` controls how the build reacts to deprecated-entity consumption; `yaml_indent` sets the indentation width of every rendered YAML artifact.

authoring_release.description: Path to a Release YAML file the LSP treats as the `current Release` context for inline diagnostics. Optional.

yaml_indent.description: Indentation width (in spaces) for every rendered YAML artifact — docker-compose files, Helm chart templates and values, and Kubernetes manifests. Defaults to 2, the conventional width for those formats.

halt_on_deprecated_severity.description: Severity, in the ordered set `warning` < `error` < `retracted`, at or above which a recorded deprecation marker halts the build. It governs both places a marker is recorded: the lockfile, for everything a build reproduces byte-for-byte, and the plugin trust record beside it, for a plugin attached in a role that returns an accept-or-reject verdict — a `plugins.governance` attachment at `ir-verdict` or `render-verdict`, and every `plugins.linter` attachment. One dial, one rule, both stores. Unset by default, and unset means no recorded marker halts: a marker is recorded against a version you already pinned, so a build that succeeded once keeps succeeding. Notification and resolution are two separate axes and neither is this dial. Every surface that reads either record reports EVERY deprecated reference it pins and every trusted plugin carrying a marker — at every severity — naming it, its severity and its message: `aggrega build`, `aggrega validate --release`, `aggrega lint --release`, the editor-facing daemon, and the AI-native build, describe and validate tools. So raising this threshold never reduces what you are told. This dial governs the build alone: it stops `aggrega build` (and the AI-native build tool, which is the same operation), while the reporting surfaces name the marker and carry on. Only a `retracted` marker affects which version a reference resolves to, and it does so when `aggrega pull` chooses a version, not at build.

plugins.description: Workspace-level Wasm plugin attachments. Each socket (governance, linter, importer) takes an array of plugin references; the build invokes each plugin's documented entry function per its socket contract. The `providers` list binds capabilities to the provider-rendering plugins that serve them.

governance.description: Governance-socket plugins. Each entry names the pipeline `role` it is attached at (`annotation-transform`, `label-transform`, `ir-verdict`, or `render-verdict`); the role fixes both what the plugin may emit and its default entry function (`annotation-transform` → `transform_annotations`; `label-transform` → `mutate`; `ir-verdict` → `verdict_ir`; `render-verdict` → `verdict_render`).

governance_append.description: Append-only addition to the effective `governance` list. Entries here are concatenated onto the resolved base list at each precedence layer, letting workspace and global configs compose governance attachments rather than shadow them.

linter.description: Linter-socket plugins. Default entry function: `lint_rules`. A linter plugin's exports are required to begin with `lint_`, so `function:` on one of these entries names an export with that prefix.

linter_append.description: Append-only addition to the effective `linter` list. Same compose-don't-shadow semantic as `governance_append`.

importer.description: Importer-socket plugins. The socket calls the `import` entry function; an attachment does not name one.

importer_append.description: Append-only addition to the effective `importer` list. Same compose-don't-shadow semantic as `governance_append`.

providers.description: Per-capability provider selections. Each entry binds one provider capability (the bare capability name a Recipe binds through `spec.capability`, e.g. `helm` or `compose`) to the bare identity of the provider-rendering plugin that serves it (a Plugin entity's `metadata.name`, the `<socket>/<name>` path, e.g. `provider/helm`), with an optional trailing `:version` in the same three forms as a version pin (bare, exact `:1.0.0`, or major-compatible range `:^1.0.0`). This is the disambiguation and override surface for a federated catalog where more than one provider plugin serves the same capability: the binding selects which publisher's plugin renders that capability. When a capability is served by exactly one provider plugin no entry is needed. Exactly one entry per capability is permitted across the composed list; a duplicate capability halts resolution loudly. Resolution is at pull: the pull records the resolved binding into the per-Release lockfile, and the build reads the lockfile — a change here after a pull is not adopted until the next pull, so build output is invariant to it (deterministic output). A missing entry for an unambiguously-served capability is not an error; a missing entry for an ambiguously-served capability halts the pull loudly, listing the candidate plugins. Version coexistence is preserved: the binding selects the plugin repository per capability, and each Recipe's own `spec.capability` version pin selects the version within that repository, so two Recipes pinning different versions of one provider still coexist.

providers_append.description: Append-only addition to the effective `providers` list. Entries here are concatenated onto the resolved base list at each precedence layer, letting workspace and global configs compose provider bindings rather than shadow them. Same compose-don't-shadow semantic as `governance_append`. The one-entry-per-capability rule applies to the composed list, so an appended entry naming a capability already bound by a lower layer halts resolution loudly.

cli.description: CLI-extension plugins installed as top-level `aggrega` commands. Each entry pins one CLI plugin by its resolved, version-pinned artifact reference and the content digest of the guest bytes that reference resolved to at install time. Unlike the four cross-cutting socket lists, whose base list whole-replaces across the config cascade, the CLI list composes: a CLI plugin in the global config registers its command(s) in every workspace, one in a workspace config registers only in that project, and both register together — so it needs no `_append` companion. The command names and help each plugin contributes come from the plugin's own self-description, read from the on-disk describe cache keyed by `digest` (a load of the guest is the fallback on a cold cache); the list carries only the pin. At command invocation the resolved bytes are re-hashed and compared to `digest`; a mismatch halts the command loudly and instructs a re-pin, so a plugin whose bytes changed since it was pinned never runs unnoticed.

lint.description: Per-rule strictness dials. Future lint sub-categories (build-time discouragement, FinOps lint, etc.) land as peer sub-blocks of `publishing_discipline`.

publishing_discipline.description: Workspace-wide gates for the publishing-linter's rule set. The `allow_*` flags relax individual discouragement checks. Artifact immutability is not configurable here: `aggrega push` refuses to overwrite a published version unconditionally.

allow_dynamic_refs.description: When true, the publishing-linter accepts $dynamicRef / $dynamicAnchor JSON Schema constructs in catalog content. Default false; these constructs are discouraged because they make compile-time schema composition non-local.

allow_id_overrides.description: When true, the publishing-linter accepts $id overrides on subschemas within an entity's schema content. Default false; $id overrides break the canonical-identifier-per-schema convention the resolver and the JSON Schema validator both rely on.

allow_direct_x_aggrega_extensions.description: When true, the build-time discouragement walker accepts x-aggrega-selector and x-aggrega-inject keywords authored directly in schema content. Default false; the recommended authoring path is usesSchema (for dependency sockets) or featuresSchema (for credential bindings), which the schema-composition layer then synthesizes into the inline extension form.

allow_aggrega_ai_prefix.description: When true, the publishing-linter accepts annotation keys using the reserved aggrega.ai/ and feature.aggrega.ai/ namespaces outside their canonical contexts. The reserved-prefix rule polices catalog-entity metadata.annotations: the bare aggrega.ai/ prefix is platform-native (well-known annotation keys are exempt regardless of this flag); the feature.aggrega.ai/ prefix is canonical on Feature kind only. Default false. Operators set this when enterprise tooling legitimately needs to use a reserved prefix; per-prefix granularity is deferred to a future iteration.

allow_nonstandard_names.description: When true, the publishing-linter accepts catalog entity names that do not follow the project's documented naming conventions. Default false; consistent naming is load-bearing for the resolver, label selection, and reviewer ergonomics.

allow_category_mismatches.description: When true, the publishing-linter suppresses the category-matches-directory rule. The standard-catalog convention requires Components under core/<category>/ to declare component.aggrega.ai/category={category} matching the directory segment, where {category} is one of the closed-set values (like ai-agent, ai-model, ai-tool, datastore, gateway, compute, ...). Workspaces with legitimate persistent exceptions opt out here. Default false.

allow_undeclared_recipe_provides.description: When true, the publishing-linter suppresses the provides-declared-by-component rule. That rule reports each key a Recipe publishes in `spec.provides` that the Component named by its `spec.implements` does not declare in the `provides` pillar of its `spec.schema`. The two are separate surfaces: what a Recipe publishes is the value a consumer receives, while what the Component declares is the output contract an `inject` `from:` reference is checked against — so a key that is published without being declared makes such a reference halt. A Recipe publishing more than its Component declares is otherwise accepted at build time, which is why the finding is advisory rather than a refusal to publish. Default false.

parse_cache.description: Daemon parse-cache eviction caps. Both caps apply simultaneously — the LRU eviction loop runs after every cache insertion and removes least-recently-used entries until both the entry count and the byte total are within bounds. Either-zero means `unbounded on that axis`, useful for CI scenarios where the cache lives only for one invocation. Distinct from `artifact_cache_dir`, which is the on-disk content cache.

max_entries.description: Cap on the number of cached parses. Default 1000. `0` disables the entry-count axis (no eviction triggered by entry count).

max_bytes.description: Cap on the cumulative len(content) bytes the cache holds. Default 100000000 (100 MB). `0` disables the byte axis (no eviction triggered by byte total).

compiled_module_cache.description: Size cap for the on-disk compiled-module cache, the machine-code store the compiler reuses so a Wasm plugin is compiled once per machine instead of once per build. It is shared across every workspace on the machine, so this key belongs in the global config file when you want one answer for the whole machine. The cap is applied once per invocation, before any plugin is loaded, by removing whole entries oldest-compiled first until the remainder fits — never while a build is compiling. Removing an entry costs a later recompile and nothing else, so the cap is safe to lower. `aggrega cache status` reports the store's current size, and `aggrega cache evict --max-size` trims it on demand to a cap given on the command line. Distinct from `artifact_cache_dir` (pulled registry content) and from `parse_cache` (the daemon's in-memory parse cache).

max_bytes.description: Cap on the bytes the compiled-module cache holds on disk. Default 53687091200 (50 GiB), a ceiling that stops unbounded growth rather than a budget meant to be felt — a single compiled plugin reaches hundreds of megabytes, so a machine that builds many plugin versions accumulates gigabytes. Set it above what one build compiles: the cap is applied before a build compiles anything, so a cap below a single build's own working set makes every build discard and recompile the same modules, and the store stops saving anything. Because the cap is applied first and the build then writes what it compiles, the store can sit above the cap between builds; it is trimmed again at the start of the next one. `0` disables the cap (the store grows without bound and nothing is ever removed automatically). Because the store is one directory every workspace shares, this cap is not per-project even when a project's own file carries it: the value resolves the same way every other key does, with the nearer file winning, but the store still has only one size. The cap in force is the one from the most recent build, so two projects capping it differently both take effect in turn, and a low cap in one discards machine code the other compiled. Setting it once in the global config file is what gives the whole machine one answer. `aggrega config show --origin` names the file each setting's effective value came from.

concurrency.description: Daemon request-dispatch concurrency settings. The daemon reads requests off a single stdin stream and runs each through a worker pool that drains a bounded request queue; responses are emitted in request arrival order regardless of completion order.

pool_size.description: Number of workers servicing the request queue. Default 4, which dispatches up to four requests concurrently; set it to 1 to run requests serially in arrival order. A value below 1 is raised to 1 when the daemon starts.

serve.description: Daemon (`aggrega serve`) behavior settings for the compiler-as-service consumed by IDE integrations.

build_on_inspect.description: Whether the daemon runs the artifact-rendering stage while inspecting an IR graph, so the advisories `aggrega build` raises while rendering also appear as editor problems. It adds none of the checks a build halts on. Nothing is written to disk either way — no rendered artifacts, no output directory, no lockfile — and the rendering stage never mutates the graph, so where the inspection answers with one it is the same graph either way. Default false, matching `aggrega inspect`: the terminal command does not reach the rendering stage while inspecting a graph, so it raises no such advisory either, and an editor inspection that raises none shows you the same thing the terminal does. Set true to ask the editor for that additional layer.

lint_on_validate.description: Whether the daemon runs the publishing-conventions check while validating a catalog entity, so the findings `aggrega lint` reports on that entity also appear as editor problems. The findings are advisory: a document that draws them still validates, and its Release still resolves and renders. Only the check that reads local content runs — no registry is consulted, nothing is fetched and nothing is written — and it is evaluated against the buffer the editor holds rather than the file on disk, so a name you correct stops being reported before you save. Default false: an editor session reports whether a document is correct, and says nothing about whether an entity is publishable, until you ask for that second layer. Set true to ask for it. Independent of this key, an editor can always ask for the check outright, which is also how the pre-publication comparison against the previously published version is reached.

mcp.description: Settings for the Model Context Protocol server (`aggrega mcp`) when it serves over HTTP rather than over the process's standard input and output. `listen` is what selects the HTTP transport; the remaining keys configure the listener it starts, and none of them is read while the server speaks over standard input and output. Distinct from `serve`, which configures the editor-backend daemon.

listen.description: Address the server listens on, which is what selects the HTTP transport. Two forms are accepted: `host:port` for a TCP address, and `unix:` followed by a filesystem path for a Unix-domain socket. `aggrega mcp --listen <address>` overrides this key for one invocation. Default empty, so no listener is started and the server speaks the protocol over standard input and output, which is what a client that launches the command as a subprocess expects. A plaintext address — one reached with no certificate and key under `tls` — is accepted only on loopback (`127.0.0.1`, `::1`, or `localhost` resolving to one of those) or on a Unix socket, which is the shape a deployment uses when a proxy in front terminates TLS; any other address is refused before anything binds, naming `mcp.tls.cert_file` and `mcp.tls.key_file`. The same two forms are the only ones accepted, certificate or not, where `authorization.trusted_proxy` is set, because a header can be trusted as a credential only where nothing but the proxy can set it.

tls.description: Certificate and key for terminating TLS inside the serving process. Set both to serve HTTPS directly from the listener `listen` names. Leave both unset to serve plaintext, which confines `listen` to loopback or a Unix socket — the shape a deployment uses when a proxy in front holds the certificate. Both keys are paths to files on disk; neither holds key material inline.

cert_file.description: Path to the PEM certificate chain the listener presents, read when the process starts. Set together with `key_file`. Default empty, so the listener serves plaintext and `listen` is confined to loopback or a Unix socket.

key_file.description: Path to the PEM private key for the certificate in `cert_file`, read when the process starts. Set together with it. A POINTER to a file, never inline key material. Default empty, so the listener serves plaintext and `listen` is confined to loopback or a Unix socket.

allowed_origins.description: Origins accepted on a request's `Origin` header. A request whose `Origin` header names an origin this list does not carry is refused with `403`; a request naming a listed origin, or carrying no `Origin` header at all, is served. Each entry is a full origin as a browser sends one — scheme, host, and the port where it is not the scheme's default — for example `https://app.example.com`. Default empty, so no origin is accepted and only a caller that sends no `Origin` header is served. A browser-based client therefore needs its origin listed here; a client that is not a browser sends no such header and needs no entry.

limits.description: Caps the HTTP listener applies to the traffic it accepts, so one caller cannot exhaust the serving process. They bound how large a single request may be, how many requests run at once, and how fast one caller may send. None of them can be turned off.

max_body_bytes.description: Largest request body the listener accepts, in bytes. A request whose body exceeds it is refused with `413`, and the body is not read past the cap. Default 4194304 (4 MiB), which sits well above a tool call carrying a whole authoring document and well below what would let one caller hold a significant share of the process's memory. The minimum is 1, so there is no value that turns the cap off; raise it where a deployment legitimately sends larger documents.

max_concurrent_requests.description: How many requests the listener runs at once. A request arriving while that many are already in flight is refused with `503` rather than queued, so a caller is told to retry instead of waiting behind work it cannot see. Default 16, which leaves room for several concurrent tool calls while keeping a small host responsive; raise it on a larger host. The minimum is 1, so there is no value that turns the cap off.

requests_per_minute.description: How many requests one caller may send in a minute. It is counted per caller rather than per deployment — against the subject the caller's token names, or against the identity a trusted proxy asserted — so one busy caller cannot spend another's allowance. A caller may send this many in a burst; the allowance then refills steadily, at one more request every `60 / requests_per_minute` seconds, and a request arriving with none left is refused with `429`. Default 120, which is two a second sustained: far above what an assistant driving a workspace sends, and still a bound on a client that has gone into a loop. The minimum is 1, so there is no value that turns the cap off.

authorization.description: What this deployment declares about the bearer tokens its callers present: which authorization server issues them, the address this deployment publishes for itself as the resource they are issued for, optionally a file to read that server's verification keys from, and optionally the headers a proxy in front sets when that proxy validates the tokens instead. `issuer` and `resource` are required whenever `listen` is set, and a listener is refused before anything binds without them; a server speaking over standard input and output reads none of these. Both are published in the OAuth protected-resource metadata document the listener serves, which is the one answer an HTTP caller receives with no credential asked for, because a client reads it in order to find out where to obtain a token. This block holds no secret material: a token is presented by a caller on the request it makes and is never a configuration field, and `jwks_file` names public verification keys rather than anything that signs.

issuer.description: Address of the authorization server that issues the tokens this deployment accepts, written as that server states its own issuer identifier — for example `https://login.example.com`. It is published in the `authorization_servers` list of the protected-resource metadata document, which is how a client learns where to obtain a token for this deployment. Default empty, which is not a usable value: a listener is refused before anything binds unless this carries a whole address, scheme and host included.

resource.description: Address this deployment publishes for itself, as a caller reaches it — for example `https://mcp.example.com/mcp`. Write the address callers actually use, including the host a proxy in front presents, because this is the identifier a client hands the authorization server when it asks for a token for this deployment, and it is published unchanged as the `resource` field of the protected-resource metadata document. Where that document is served is derived from it, by inserting `/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource` between the host and the path: a deployment published as `https://mcp.example.com/mcp` serves it at `https://mcp.example.com/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource/mcp`, and also at that well-known path with nothing after it, which is where a client looks second. A token is accepted only where this address is among the audiences it names. Default empty, which is not a usable value: a listener is refused before anything binds unless this carries a whole address, scheme and host included.

jwks_file.description: Path to a file holding the JSON Web Key Set the tokens this deployment accepts are verified against, read when the process starts. Default empty, which is the usual case: the keys are read from the authorization server itself, by asking `issuer` where it publishes them and fetching them from the address it names, and they are re-read once when a token arrives signed by a key identifier the held set does not carry. Set this where the workspace is offline, in which case a listener is refused before anything binds without it, because an offline workspace makes no network request and there is no other way to obtain the keys; the file then holds the only keys accepted, and the authorization server is never contacted. The file holds PUBLIC verification keys and never anything that signs. A relative path resolves against the directory of the config file that declared it.

trusted_proxy.description: Read who a caller is from headers a proxy in front sets, instead of validating a bearer token here. Set this only where a proxy in front validates tokens itself AND nothing but that proxy can reach the listener: with it set, `listen` must be loopback or a Unix socket, and any other address is refused before anything binds, naming both settings. A header is trustworthy exactly as far as the set of callers that can set it, and on an address the network reaches every caller can set any header it likes, so a listener in this mode on such an address would let every caller claim to be anyone. With this set no token is read at all — not from the `Authorization` header, not from anywhere else, and no key set is fetched — the caller's identity is the value of `principal_header`, a request that does not carry that header is answered `401`, and the two headers named here are the only ones read. Leave it out, which is the default, and this server validates bearer tokens itself.

principal_header.description: Header the proxy in front puts the caller's identity in — for example `X-Forwarded-User`. Its value is taken exactly as written and compared to nothing, in the same way the subject of a token this server validates itself is recorded and compared to nothing. It is the whole credential in this mode, so it is required whenever `trusted_proxy` is set, and a request arriving without it is answered `401`.

scopes_header.description: Header the proxy in front puts the caller's granted scopes in, separated by spaces — for example `X-Forwarded-Scopes`. Default empty, which asserts no scopes for any caller. Whatever it is called, no header other than this one and `principal_header` is read.

deny_reach.description: Kinds of reach this deployment does not carry, whatever a caller's token says. Every operation declares how far its own effects travel — `none` for one that reads or renders and leaves nothing behind, `workspace` for one that writes inside the workspace this process serves, `registry` for one that publishes, signs or withdraws, and `machine` for one that changes what every workspace on the host shares — and naming a kind here withdraws every tool of that kind from this deployment. A withdrawn tool is absent from the tool list and from what `describe-capabilities` answers, for every caller, and calling it anyway is refused naming this setting, because no scope could admit it. Default empty, so a deployment carries whatever its callers' scopes admit. This is a bound the deployment sets on itself, on top of the per-caller bound scopes set: a deployment that serves reads and nothing else names the three writing kinds here and then cannot publish even to a caller whose token carries every scope. Naming `machine` is accepted and changes nothing — no tool of that kind is offered over HTTP at all, which is a property of the transport rather than a setting. Read while the listener starts: a value outside the four is refused when the configuration loads, and changing it takes a restart. Not read at all while the server speaks over standard input and output, where the caller is the person who launched the process.

health.description: Where a supervisor asks whether this process is alive and whether it is ready to answer a call. The two checks are answered on an address of their own and never on the address `listen` names: every request to the endpoint carries a bearer token, so a probe answered there would hand anything that can reach the endpoint an unauthenticated reading of the process together with a free way to make it work. The endpoint answers `/healthz` and `/readyz` with the same `404` it gives every path it does not serve, with a token and without one alike.

listen.description: Address the liveness and readiness checks are answered on, in the same two forms `listen` takes: `host:port`, or `unix:` followed by a filesystem path. Default empty, so no second listener is started and neither check is answered anywhere. With an address set, `GET /healthz` is answered `200` from the moment the process is running, and `GET /readyz` is answered `503` until the workspace has resolved and the endpoint has bound and `200` from then on — which is the distinction a supervisor needs, since a process that is up is not yet a process that can answer a call. Every answer is a status code with an empty body, no token is asked for and no header is read; any other path on this address is `404`, and any other method on these two is `405`. Unlike `listen` this address is not confined to loopback or a Unix socket and no address is refused for it: point it at one of those, which is what it is for, and note that whatever can reach the address you choose can read those two answers.

registries.description: Per-registry settings and signature trust policy, keyed by registry host. A registry not listed here uses the defaults: a present signature is verified and an absent signature is tolerated, except for `hub.aggrega.ai`, whose embedded baseline mandates a verified signature even with no explicit entry. An explicit entry for a host overrides that host's baseline.

signing.description: Top-level signing block, applying to all registries: the keyless service URLs, an optional keyed-key path, and the all-registries trust stance (`required` and `kinds`). A per-registry `signing` block overrides the endpoint defaults for that host and carries the same `required`/`kinds` stance scoped to that host — one name, one job, scope from placement. The top-level `required`/`kinds` policy composes monotonically across the config cascade. SECURITY: this block holds no secret material — the OIDC identity token is never a config field (it is supplied at runtime via flag or the ambient OIDC environment) and `key_path` is a path to a key file, never inline key bytes.

RegistryConfig.description: Settings and signature trust policy scoped to one OCI registry host.

host.description: The registry host these settings apply to (e.g. `hub.aggrega.ai`). Matched against the registry host of the push/pull target.

name.description: Optional friendly alias for this registry. The host is the identity; `name` is a convenience selector that resolves to this entry's host wherever a registry is named (for example `--registry`). An alias must be unique across entries.

trusted_identities.description: OR-set of keyless signing identities accepted for artifacts pulled from this registry. A signature verifies when its certificate matches any one entry. Used by the keyless verification path.

trusted_deprecation_identities.description: OR-set of keyless identities additionally accepted to sign a retroactive deprecation marker for an artifact pulled from this registry. A deprecation marker is honored when its signature matches the original artifact's signer OR any entry here — so a registry owner or a security team can retract an artifact the original publisher can no longer reach, without being trusted to sign the artifacts themselves. Used only by the deprecation discovery path; it never widens the trust set for artifact signatures.

public_key.description: Pinned cosign-compatible public-key PEM (inline) for a keyed-mode registry. When set, signatures from this registry are verified offline against this key rather than against keyless identities.

trusted_root.description: Optional path to a pinned Sigstore trust-root bundle for air-gapped keyless verification. When set, the keyless trust anchor is loaded from this file with no network; when empty, the public-good trust root is fetched and cached.

advisory.description: When true, a signature verification failure for this registry is downgraded to a warning rather than halting the pull. Verification still runs and the failure is reported; the pull proceeds. Defaults to false.

skip_signature_verification.description: Per-host break-glass opt-out from signature verification — the same `skip_signature_verification` switch as the global one, scoped by placement to this host. It does NOT defeat the top-level `signing.required` policy: an org-required signature is still verified on this host regardless of this switch; only the global switch can disable that. Setting this together with a per-registry `signing.required` on the same host is the allowed-but-perverse push-required + pull-skip combination — the skip wins on the verify side, since a per-host required stance (unlike the top-level one) is not immune to the per-host skip. Defaults to false.

signing.description: This registry's signing block: the keyless service URLs, an optional keyed-key path, and the per-host trust stance. The endpoint fields override the global `signing` block for pushes to this host; a CLI flag overrides both. `required` and `kinds` read from placement — under a registry entry they scope the one trust stance to this host (publishing an in-scope unsigned artifact is refused, and consuming an unsigned one is refused), the same concept the top-level `signing` block carries for all registries.

SigningConfig.description: A signing block: the keyless service URLs, an optional pointer to a keyed-key file, and the trust stance (`required` and `kinds`). Placed at the top level it applies to all registries; placed under a `registries[]` entry it applies to that host — every field reads its scope from placement. `required` is one trust stance covering both directions (an unsigned in-scope push is refused and an unsigned in-scope pull is refused). SECURITY: holds no secret material — the OIDC identity token is never a config field (short-lived, supplied at runtime), and `key_path` is a path to a key file, never inline key bytes. This mirrors the verify side's asymmetry: an inline `public_key` is allowed there, but the sign side carries only a key PATH.

fulcio_url.description: Fulcio certificate-authority URL for keyless signing. When unset, the public-good Fulcio instance is used.

rekor_url.description: Rekor transparency-log URL for keyless signing. When unset, the public-good Rekor instance is used.

timestamp_url.description: RFC3161 timestamp-authority URL for keyless signing. When unset, the public-good timestamp authority is used.

key_path.description: Path to a held ECDSA P-256 private-key PEM file for offline keyed signing. A POINTER to a file, never inline key material. When unset, the keyless path is used.

required.description: The one trust stance for this block's scope: when true, publishing an in-scope artifact kind requires a signature (an unsigned in-scope push is refused) AND consuming one requires a signature (an unsigned in-scope pull is refused). Scope reads from placement — on the top-level `signing` block it covers every registry; under a `registries[]` entry's `signing` block it covers that one host. One name, one job, both scopes. The top-level policy composes monotonically across the config cascade — any layer that sets it true makes it effective true, and no lower-precedence layer can turn it back off — so it cannot be removed by an ordinary config edit. Defaults to false.

kinds.description: Scopes `required` to specific artifact kinds. Empty or a single `all` entry means every signable kind; otherwise the stance applies to exactly the listed kinds, matching the entity `kind:` value (e.g. `Component`, `Feature`, `Recipe`, `FeatureRecipe`, `SchemaLibrary`, `MappingLibrary`, `Aggregate`, `Plugin`). On the top-level `signing` block it composes as a union across the cascade — a layer can widen the scope but never shrink it. Scope reads from placement, the same as `required`.

TrustedIdentity.description: One acceptable keyless signing identity: a certificate subject (the OIDC identity) paired with the OIDC issuer that vouched for it.

identity.description: Exact certificate subject alternative name — the OIDC identity bound into the short-lived signing certificate (e.g. a maintainer email or a CI workflow URI).

identity_regexp.description: Regular expression matched against the certificate subject, used instead of an exact `identity` (e.g. to accept any workflow under an organization).

issuer.description: OIDC issuer URL that issued the identity token (e.g. `https://accounts.google.com` or `https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com`).

PluginRef.description: Reference to a Wasm plugin attached at a socket whose entry function the attachment may name — the `governance` and `linter` lists. The sockets whose entry point is fixed instead use `FixedEntryPluginRef`, which carries these same fields without `function`. `uri` and `capability` together select the plugin: `uri` only is a direct attach (the plugin at that identity is attached verbatim — the cross-cutting sockets' path, since their plugins declare no served capabilities); `capability` only resolves the plugin serving that capability (the bare capability name a Recipe binds through `spec.capability`, e.g. `helm`); both together disambiguate — `capability` names what to resolve and `uri` selects which publisher's plugin serves it, by that plugin's bare identity, in a federated catalog where more than one plugin serves the capability. `function` overrides the socket's default entry function; when omitted, the socket's documented default applies — on a governance entry that default follows from `role`. `role` names the governance attachment role and is read on a governance entry only. `with` carries optional attachment-time inputs the plugin reads.

uri.description: Plugin identifier: a Plugin entity's bare identity — the `<socket>/<name>` path, e.g. `governance/redact` or `provider/helm` — a local filesystem path, or a registry alias. Optional: an entry may instead select the plugin by `capability`. An optional trailing `:version` pins the version in the same three forms as any version pin (bare, exact `:1.0.0`, or major-compatible range `:^1.0.0`).

role.description: The pipeline role a governance attachment is bound to, read on a `governance` entry only: `annotation-transform` injects annotations onto resolved components before annotation expansion, so bound injections become Feature attachments; `label-transform` auto-tags topology-graph node labels at topology construction; `ir-verdict` renders an accept/reject verdict over the IR graph at static analysis; `render-verdict` renders a verdict over the rendered artifacts at rendering. The role — not the plugin's declared kind — fixes what the plugin may emit: a verdict role's output can only be read as a verdict, never applied as a change; a transform role's output is host-confined to its facet (annotations or labels). It also selects the default entry function (`annotation-transform` → `transform_annotations`; `label-transform` → `mutate`; `ir-verdict` → `verdict_ir`; `render-verdict` → `verdict_render`).

capability.description: The provider capability this entry selects a plugin for — the bare capability name a Recipe binds through `spec.capability` (e.g. `helm`, `compose`). Optional: an entry may instead attach a plugin directly by `uri`. The provider bindings use this to select which publisher's plugin serves a capability in a federated catalog; the cross-cutting sockets leave it empty and attach by `uri`.

function.description: Optional override for the socket's default entry function. When omitted, the socket's documented default applies (governance `annotation-transform` → `transform_annotations`, governance `label-transform` → `mutate`, governance `ir-verdict` → `verdict_ir`, governance `render-verdict` → `verdict_render`, linter → `lint_rules`). The override may name any export the plugin declares, and the export it names must return the output shape that socket reads: the build halts when that output carries a top-level field the shape does not declare, naming the export called and the unexpected field. The check reads which top-level field names are present, not which are absent or what nests beneath them, so it is not a full validation of the output.

with.description: Optional attachment-time inputs the plugin reads. Both members are optional and socket-agnostic, so any socket may reuse this surface.

FixedEntryPluginRef.description: Reference to a Wasm plugin attached at a socket whose entry point is fixed rather than named by the attachment — the `importer` list and the `providers` bindings. It carries the same fields as `PluginRef` without `function`: the importer socket calls the one entry function its socket contract names, and a provider drives a fixed set of phase-keyed exports rather than one selectable entry, so on neither list is there an entry for `function` to name and the key is not accepted there. `uri` and `capability` together select the plugin: `uri` only is a direct attach (the plugin at that identity is attached verbatim — the importer socket's path, since its plugins declare no served capabilities); `capability` only resolves the plugin serving that capability (the bare capability name a Recipe binds through `spec.capability`, e.g. `helm`); both together disambiguate — `capability` names what to resolve and `uri` selects which publisher's plugin serves it, by that plugin's bare identity, in a federated catalog where more than one plugin serves the capability. `role` is accepted here but read on neither list this shape serves: the governance attachment role it names is read on a `governance` entry, which uses `PluginRef`, so a role set on one of these entries has no effect. `with` carries optional attachment-time inputs the plugin reads; a provider binding takes its render configuration from the Recipe instead, so `with:` on one is refused at load.

uri.description: Plugin identifier: a Plugin entity's bare identity — the `<socket>/<name>` path, e.g. `governance/redact` or `provider/helm` — a local filesystem path, or a registry alias. Optional: an entry may instead select the plugin by `capability`. An optional trailing `:version` pins the version in the same three forms as any version pin (bare, exact `:1.0.0`, or major-compatible range `:^1.0.0`).

role.description: The governance attachment role. Neither list that uses this shape reads it — the role is read on a `governance` entry, and those entries use `PluginRef` — so a role set here is accepted and has no effect. The permitted values are the four governance roles, and what each one means is described on `PluginRef`.

capability.description: The provider capability this entry selects a plugin for — the bare capability name a Recipe binds through `spec.capability` (e.g. `helm`, `compose`). Optional: an entry may instead attach a plugin directly by `uri`. The provider bindings use this to select which publisher's plugin serves a capability in a federated catalog; the cross-cutting sockets leave it empty and attach by `uri`.

with.description: Optional attachment-time inputs the plugin reads. Both members are optional and socket-agnostic, so any socket may reuse this surface.

CLIPluginRef.description: A pinned CLI-extension plugin installed as a top-level `aggrega` command: the resolved, version-pinned artifact reference the command resolves and runs, and the content digest of the guest bytes that reference resolved to at install time. Together they pin exactly which bytes the command executes; the digest also keys the describe cache that supplies the command's names and help without loading the guest.

uri.description: The resolved, version-pinned artifact reference the command resolves and runs, e.g. `oci://hub.aggrega.ai/plugin/cli/<name>:1.2.0`, pinned at install.

digest.description: The hex SHA-256 content digest of the guest `.wasm` bytes the reference resolved to at install. It pins the exact bytes the command runs — a later resolution whose bytes hash differently halts the command — and is the key into the describe cache that renders the command's help without loading the guest.

PluginRefWith.description: Optional attachment-time inputs a plugin reads. Both members are optional and the surface is general, so any socket may reuse it.

sources.description: Definition file paths the host reads at compile time and hands to the plugin. Each entry is a filesystem path resolved against the declaring config file's directory.

settings.description: Free-form settings object handed to the plugin verbatim. The host does not interpret its shape; the plugin defines the keys it reads.
